lessons.title: Synthesis — two at a time
lessons.gloss: synthesis — a four-turn exchange carried almost entirely by pronouns, and what that does to how it sounds

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: "I tell it to him," in three words. (Se lo digo.)
— ¿Tienes el libro? — Sí. ¿Te lo digo? — Sí, y se lo dices a Ana. — Y la comida — se la hago hoy.

Look at the last three lines. After the first sentence names the book, not one noun does any work. Te lo, se lo, se la — six words that name nothing, and the conversation is perfectly clear to both speakers.

That is what all of this has been for. Fifteen chapters of object pronouns exist so that a conversation can stop repeating itself, and this is the point where the machinery is complete enough to see it happen.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: two words carrying a whole sentence

segments.text: Se la hago is three words and it means "I make the meal for her, today." Two of the three are pronouns; between them they carry a person and a thing, neither of which is named anywhere in the sentence.
English cannot compress like this. I'll make it for her needs five words and still spells out for. Spanish puts both jobs in front of the verb, in a fixed order, and gets on with it.

The cost is the one you already know, doubled. Two pronouns are two promises that both things are still in the room. When you lose track of one of them, the sentence does not become wrong — it becomes about somebody else, and nobody will notice until it matters.
So the practice that pays here is not conjugation. It is keeping a conversation's furniture in mind while you talk.

segments.prompt: Say shall I tell it to you.
Say I make it for her, about la comida.

feedback.correct: Three words, a person and a thing, neither named.
feedback.incorrect: Se la hago — le becomes se in front of la.

segments.prompt: In se la hago, how many of the three words name anything?

feedback.correct: And it is still completely clear to both speakers.
feedback.incorrect: None. Both the person and the thing are carried by pronouns.

segments.prompt: You lose track of which thing se la points at. Does the sentence become wrong?
acceptedResponses: no, it becomes about something else
it stays grammatical but means something else

feedback.correct: Which is harder to notice than being wrong.
feedback.incorrect: No. It stays grammatical and quietly becomes about something else.

segments.text: "I make it for her"? (Se la hago.) How many nouns are in that sentence? (None.) And what does each pronoun promise? (That its thing is still in the room.) Next: the past tense.
